paper_title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Foundation models for biomolecular structure. Predicting the three-dimensional structure of protein from its sequence [1] is now routine computation. AlphaFold [2, 3] and RoseTTAFold [4] predict single chains from multiple sequence alignments, in many cases with accuracy comparable to experiment. ESMFold [5] and OmegaFold [6] replace the alignment with the representations of protein language model trained on sequences alone [7, 8]. Prediction has since moved from single chains to assemblies: AlphaFold-Multimer [9] predicts protein complexes, and AlphaFold 3 [10], RoseTTAFold All-Atom [11], Chai-1 [12], Boltz [13, 14] and OpenDDE [15] model proteins together with nucleic acids and small molecules. The architectures have also become simpler and generative. AlphaFlow [16] turns structure predictor into flow-matching model [17], and SimpleFold [18] folds proteins with standard transformer trained by flow matching. Related models design backbones [19, 20], design sequences for given backbone [21], and model sequence, structure and function jointly [22, 23]. These models now serve as foundation models for structural biology. Each of them, however, maps fixed kind of input to fixed kind of output. None takes an instruction in natural language, uses what is written about protein, or explains its answer. Large language models. Large language models (LLMs) have developed along different path. Transformers trained on text at scale [2427] follow instructions, answer questions across scientific disciplines, and reason step by step in natural language [28, 29]. Equipped with tools [30], they plan and carry out multi-step research tasks in chemistry [31, 32] and biology [3335]. They do not, however, produce molecular structure by themselves. When we ask four frontier chat models to write the C𝛼 coordinates of protein without tools, their mean TM-scores lie between 0.147 and 0.224, against 0.1380.149 for random-walk reference on the same targets (Section 4.4). The gap between the two. The abilities of biomolecular foundation models are therefore important to science but are not yet part of general-purpose LLMs. Existing work connects the two in three ways. In the first, an LLM agent calls folding or design program as an external tool and reads back its output [3437]. The language model chooses what to run, but its reasoning stays outside the predictor and can affect prediction only through the predictors fixed inputs. In the second, protein encoder is attached to an LLM so that the model can answer questions about sequence or structure in text [3842], following visionlanguage models [4345]. These models describe proteins and do not generate coordinates. In the third, structure is converted into discrete tokens that language model reads and writes [4649], or continuous generator is attached to sequence model [50, 51], as generative heads are attached to language models for images and robot actions [5254]. In all three, the reasoning that an LLM carries out in language has not been shown to improve the structure that is predicted. Our goal. Calpha is project to build general-purpose LLM in which these abilities are native. One model should fold proteins and predict complexes, and it should understand protein sequence and structure well enough to discuss them. The abilities that today belong to separate biomolecular foundation models would then be part of general model and connected to everything else that it knows. Most importantly, we want the models natural-language reasoning to take part in the prediction. What the model reads in the literature, what scientist tells it and what it infers about mechanism should influence, and in some cases determine, the structure it predicts. model of this kind could be asked for the bound state of protein, or could revise prediction after reasoning about why it is wrong. We see this as route to better scientific discovery with LLMs. This goal has not been reached. Section 7.3 lays out the roadmap, and this report covers its first step. This report: single-chain structures from an LLM. The first step is to make an LLM output the structure of single protein chain. In Calpha (Figure 1), Qwen3.5-9B [55] reads protein sequence inside an ordinary chat turn, together with residue features from ESM2-3B [5]. For question about the protein, it replies in text. For folding request, it emits <structure> token, and its hidden states at the residue positions condition pretrained SimpleFold-3B flow-matching head [18] that generates all-atom coordinates. The head receives information about the protein only through the language model. The same forward pass therefore decides whether to fold and supplies what the head folds from, with no tool call. The question we can answer at this stage is how much folding accuracy is retained when the structure head receives its input through the chat model. Figure 1. Calpha inference and training. Frozen ESM2 features enter Qwen at the amino-acid positions. When Qwen emits <structure>, the front-end mixes residue states from nine layers to condition SimpleFold-3B. Joint training updates Qwen, the input adapter and 100M folding head. The second stage freezes Qwen and the pretrained 3B head and trains the 8.4Mparameter conditioning front-end. What we find. We report three observations. First, the states exported from Qwen support single-chain folding: the head reaches mean TM-scores of 0.808 on our development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on CAMEO-style set. Second, the current Calpha configuration scores lower than the direct ESM2 SimpleFold3B baseline on chains of 300600 residues in all three sets. At 100299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. The two systems also differ in which weights they update, in training duration and in crop length  (Table 2)  , so the comparison measures their combined effect. Third, four of the five tested folding request types elicited the trigger on every evaluated sequence. Accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset [56] fell by 7.1 percentage points after protein training. What remains open. These results concern single chains scored on C𝛼 atoms under one fixed request. Calpha does not yet predict complexes, and it does not yet take structure as input. In none of our comparisons does routing through the language model make folding more accurate than the direct ESM2 baseline. Whether change of wording preserves coordinate accuracy, and whether an instruction or line of reasoning can steer the predicted conformation, are the questions that the goal above depends on. They are open (Section 7).

sections.title: 2 System and training
sections.content: Calpha has four parts that run at inference: protein encoder, chat model, small conditioning front-end and structure head. Two of them, the encoder and the head, are pretrained specialist models used with their public weights. We first describe the inference path, then the two training stages, and Table 1 states for every component where its weights come from and when it is trained. 2.

sections.title: Inference path
sections.content: Input. The vocabulary of Qwen3.5-9B [55] is extended with amino-acid tokens and <structure> token. protein is written as span of amino-acid tokens inside an ordinary chat turn. Frozen ESM2-3B [5] computes per-residue features, which small adapter (a learned mixture over ESM2 layers, an MLP and zero-initialised gate) maps to the model width and adds to the embeddings of the corresponding amino-acid tokens. The language model therefore sees each residue as its letter plus what ESM2 knows about it. ESM2 is thus second model that reads the sequence; what the design guarantees is that its features reach the structure head only through the language model. Trigger. The language head is unchanged. Emitting the token <structure> invokes the structure head; otherwise the language model continues generating text. Section 5 measures this decision. Whether to fold is thus decided by the model itself, in the same forward pass as any other answer. 3 Table 1. Components of Calpha: where the weights come from, what is trained in each stage, and what runs at inference. dash means the component is not present in that stage. Component (parameters) Initial weights Stage 1 Stage 2 At inference ESM2-3B encoder Adapter, ESM2 to language model Qwen3.5-9B (9B) SimpleFold-100M head (0.1B) Conditioning front-end (8.4M) SimpleFold-3B head (2.86B) public new public public new public frozen trained trained trained frozen frozen frozen trained frozen yes yes yes Calpha-Joint only yes yes Conditioning front-end. After the trigger we read the hidden states at the residue positions from nine layers of the 32-layer model (layers 0, 4, , 32; width 4096). This gives tensor of shape (𝐿, 9, 4096), the same form as the per-layer ESM2 tensor that SimpleFold consumes. The front-end is SimpleFolds own conditioning entry, rebuilt for this shape: learned softmax mixture over the nine layers followed by projection into the head. It has 8.4M parameters. Structure head. The head is SimpleFold-3B (2.86B parameters) with its public weights: an atom encoder, residue trunk and an atom decoder trained with flow matching to transport Gaussian noise to all-atom coordinates. We sample with 200 steps and the default noise scale (𝜏 = 0.01) and report single sample per target. The head outputs all atoms, but every accuracy number in this report is computed on alpha carbons only; side-chain accuracy was not evaluated.

sections.title: 2.2 Training
sections.content: Stage 1: teach the language model to read proteins and to decide when to fold. All parameters of Qwen3.59B, the ESM2 adapter and small SimpleFold-100M head, initialised from its public weights, are trained jointly for 2B counted tokens. The loss is the sum of three terms: the language cross-entropy, the cross-entropy of the trigger token, and the heads flow-matching loss with smooth-lDDT term, the last weighted by 28.9 to match gradient scales. The language side mixes 75% protein tasks (inverse folding, secondary structure, contact prediction, infilling) with 25% general text and reasoning data, all in English; the structure side uses 84,658 PDB chains cropped to 256 residues. The stage-1 model with its 100M head is itself working folding model and we report it as Calpha-Joint. In trained parameters this stage is by far the larger of the two. Stage 2: attach large pretrained head and train only the front-end. The language model is frozen and exports hidden states. The 100M head is replaced by SimpleFold-3B, which is also frozen; only the rebuilt frontend is trained, for 20,000 steps at an effective batch size of 64 (learning rate 104, EMA 0.999) on the same 84,658 chains, followed by further 10,000 steps with the crop length raised from 256 to 512 residues. The whole stage took about 11 hours on eight H200 GPUs. The figure of 8.4M trained parameters describes this stage only: the language model whose hidden states it reads was trained in full in stage 1.

sections.content: In our ESM2 SimpleFold-3B baseline, ESM2-3B encodes the sequence into residue features. fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head takes those features directly and generates the atomic coordinates. In Calpha, the ESM2 features first pass through Qwen. trained projection maps Qwens residue states to the inputs of frozen SimpleFold-3B head. Every target is searched against one training pool of 667,331 chains (PDB [59] plus AFDBSwissProt [60]) and classified using minimum sequence identity of 30% and coverage of at least 50% on either side, then assigned to homolog or no-homolog bucket. Scorer outputs also include nonlocal C𝛼 proximity and normalized radius of gyration where available; none of these checks validates side-chain geometry. Paired comparisons. For each target we subtract the reference systems TM-score from Calphas. We report the mean difference and percentile 95% interval from 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples of entries. The intervals quantify variation across entries for one trained model per configuration. Related sequences and multiple CASP entries from single target can reduce the effective sample size. Interval estimates condition on these training runs. Frontier chat models. GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek are asked, with one fixed English prompt and no tools, to return an alpha-carbon-only PDB file for the sequence. Because of cost they are run on fixed, lengthstratified subset of 180 targets (60 per set, at most 300 residues), and every other system is rescored on the same subset for comparison. Baseline checks. Appendix distinguishes paper-level reproductions, checks against earlier runs, and baselines evaluated only under our protocol. Those distinctions apply to the model comparisons throughout Section 4.

sections.content: ESM2 SimpleFold-3B reaches 0.822, 0.682 and 0.917. sections.title: 5 Language behavior
sections.content: Section 4 measured folding under fixed request. In conversation, the user can instead ask question about the same sequence, for which invoking the structure head would be an error. We test whether Qwen makes that distinction under different wordings. separate before-and-after comparison measures how much general question-answering accuracy it retains after protein training. Deciding when to fold. For each eligible sequence we evaluate five folding requests and one protein question that calls for text answer. Table 6 reports the rates. Four request types elicited the trigger throughout the evaluated examples; the fifth elicited it on 95.598.2% across the sets. False triggers on the text questions ranged from 0 to 1.4%. Appendix describes the length filter and the resulting counts. An earlier model trained on mixed ChineseEnglish data that also contained fold into structure tokens tasks triggered on 5% of plain English requests. With the architecture held fixed, the next run removed those token-folding tasks and used English throughout. Triggering improved within the first quarter of training. The two data changes were made together. General ability. On pre-registered 350-item subset of MMLU-Pro [56, 63], harder successor of MMLU [64], with five-shot chain-of-thought prompting, the base Qwen3.5-9B scores 0.774 and the stage-1 language model scores 0.703. Accuracy fell by 7.1 percentage points. The trained model still produced answers in the expected format. Reducing the share of general data from 25% to 15% cost further five points on the same test without improving folding. From the trigger to structure. paraphrase can elicit the same trigger while changing the residue states read by the head. The rates in Table 6 therefore establish how often each request invokes folding. Measuring the fraction of requests that actually return full-length structure, and the TM-score of those structures, requires following the same requests through coordinate generation and scoring. 8 Table 6. On CASP16, single sample scores 0.635. Selecting the sample most similar to the others gives 0.642. An oracle that sees the reference structure reaches 0.679, close to the direct systems single-sample score of 0.682. The oracle bounds selection within these draws. Across targets, agreement among samples correlates with true TM (Spearman 0.8530.893 across sets). Using that agreement to assign calibrated confidence to new target remains to be tested.

sections.title: 7.1 Scope of the evidence
sections.content: The strongest length-dependent finding applies to the two trained systems in Table 2. Their paired gap is negative at 300600 residues on all three sets. matched comparison that fixes the trainable head parameters, optimizer schedule and training crops across both conditioning paths would identify the contribution of the path under that recipe. Explaining whether errors arise in local structure or in the arrangement of distant regions also requires measurements across targets. The reported scores assess C𝛼 structure for isolated chains or domains. Table 10 reports the fraction of adjacent C𝛼 distances in the physical range. random walk constructed with physical step lengths also passes this check. Side-chain placement, all-atom steric quality, complexes, inference latency and peak inference memory remain unevaluated. Third-party training cutoffs and baseline reproduction checks vary by model (Appendix C). Folding accuracy was measured with one request template. Request recognition under paraphrases establishes language-interface capability. It leaves open whether the residue states produced by those phrasings generate structures of comparable accuracy.

sections.title: 7.2 Relation to earlier systems
sections.content: Single-sequence predictors such as ESMFold [5] and OmegaFold [6] use protein language-model features to fold sequence. SimpleFold [18] generates coordinates with flow-matching transformer. Calpha uses its pretrained head and supplies the conditioning features through Qwen. Protein chat models such as ProtLLM [39] and ProteinGPT [40] answer questions in text. BioMatrix [48] and Trion-1 [49] also generate discrete structure tokens. ESM3 [22] and DPLM-2 [23] use discrete representations for joint sequence and structure modelling. UniGenX [50] and HD-Prot [51] attach continuous generators to sequence models. Calpha combines chat interface with continuous head: the same language model decides when to fold and supplies the residue states used to generate coordinates. chat agent invoking an external folding program is another way to handle these requests [35, 36]. Comparing the two interfaces remains open.

sections.title: 7.3 Availability and outlook
sections.content: The code, the per-target scores and the scorer are available in the code repository. Figure 5 places single-chain folding within the projects longer-term goals. Conclusion. Biomolecular foundation models and LLMs have so far been combined mainly through tool calls or text-only interfaces. Calpha aims to make structure prediction and structure understanding native abilities of general-purpose LLM, so that reasoning in language can shape what is predicted. This report takes the first step. Qwen learns when to invoke folding across several English requests, and its residue states support single-chain folding under the fixed benchmark request. We observe two limitations in these runs. After protein training, accuracy is lower on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset, and the final configuration scores lower than the ESM2 SimpleFold-3B baseline on chains of 300600 residues in all three sets. It also leaves the central part of the goal untested. Routing through the language model has not made folding more accurate, and we have not measured whether an instruction or line of reasoning changes the predicted coordinates. The next steps are to match the training recipes so that the long-chain gap can be explained, to evaluate folding online across phrasings, and to extend the model to complexes and to structure as an input (Figure 5). sections.content: This appendix gives the experiments behind Section 6. All development results are FoldBench evaluations with one prediction per scored target. Figure 2 labels each trained configuration with the date of its evaluation. Random is random-walk baseline with no learned parameters, and the randomly initialised head (Scratch) is evaluated at step 1,667. The joint-training run in the figure (0.750) predates the checkpoint reported as CalphaJoint in Table 4 (0.744). B.1 Replacing token output by continuous head At two billion training tokens, the early Qwen model generated ESM3 tokens by greedy decoding. The mean across 333 scored chains was 0.5617. The Calpha-Token checkpoint used in the main benchmark also saw two billion training tokens, but was trained separately to write DPLM-2 tokens. It averaged 0.6623 on its 333 completed chains. Both token runs lacked score for 8uxt_A. Applying the main benchmarks zero-for-failure rule gives 0.6603 across all 334 chains. The 0.562 and 0.660 labels therefore describe different checkpoints, token representations and scoring populations. For the 100M-head experiment we kept the ESM3-token backbone frozen and trained pretrained SimpleFold100M head on its hidden states for 10,000 steps. The head starts from the public SimpleFold-100M weights, so part of the gain may come from its structural pretraining and not from the continuous output form. With the 100M head, states from Qwen without protein training yielded nearly the same mean TM as one-hot sequence input (paired ΔTM +0.0003, CI [0.007, +0.008]). In separate 3B-head configuration, ESM2 features injected through trained projector gave 0.476 with Qwen that had received no protein training. The input representation and head size both matter when interpreting this comparison. B.2 Historical comparisons with ESM2-conditioned SimpleFold heads On FoldBench-334, the 100M-head comparison gave paired difference of 0.077 TM (CI [0.090, 0.064]). With the 3B head fine-tuned on both paths for 10,000 steps at crop 256, the historical comparison gave 0.031 (CI [0.048, 0.015]). The final comparison in Table 9 includes the changes to training listed in Table 2. Each interval pertains to its own configuration. B.3 Co-training and structural pretraining Training the language model jointly with the 100M head, instead of freezing it, raised TM from 0.712 to 0.750 (paired +0.038, CI [+0.023, +0.053]; +0.052 on the no-homolog bucket). Two controls from the same experiment bound what the result depends on. head initialised at random instead of from the SimpleFold weights reached only 0.270 at the step where the pretrained head reached 0.672. The pretrained head scored higher on all 334 targets at that checkpoint. run without ESM2 input was stopped early; its in-training probes were at 0.260.32 against 0.370.57 for the main run at matched steps, which is suggestive but not formal result. The stage-1 language evaluation is reported in Section 5. B.4 Effect of unfreezing the pretrained head Swapping in the 3B head and retraining it on our 84,658 chains gave 0.791. Freezing it and training only the 8.4M-parameter front-end gave 0.801 (paired +0.0105, CI [+0.002, +0.020]); this comparison also changed the stage-1 language model that supplies the hidden states, so the gain cannot be attributed to freezing alone. OpenDDE is run with its command-line defaults (five samples, top-ranked reported) with and without an MSA. The MSAs come from the public ColabFold server [65] with no date filter on the sequence databases, so the MSA row is an upper reference and not held-out result. The 155 CASP16 domains correspond to 72 distinct sequences; OpenDDE is run once per sequence. Frontier chat models. The model identifiers are gpt-6.1-sol, claude-opus-5-5, gemini-4-argon and deepseek-v4.1-flash, queried on 2026-11-11 with default reasoning settings and no tools. The DeepSeek responses come from two endpoints serving the same model (87 targets through gateway, 93 through the vendor API). Parseable output was returned for 180 (GPT), 172 (Claude), 179 (Gemini) and 176 (DeepSeek) of the 180 targets; the rest score zero. Eligible sequences for the trigger test. The trigger evaluation only forms prompts for sequences of at most 400 residues. This leaves 278, 140 and 155 eligible entries for FoldBench-334, CASP16 and CAMEO-2025, and these are the denominators of the rates in Table 6. The rates for the fifth request type correspond to 273/278, 135/140 and 148/155.
